opeds.headline: Don't Ration the Future in the Name of Caution
opeds.subtitle: Freezing AI to soothe institutions leaves patients, workers, and families in scarcity.
opeds.body:
A child in a county hospital waits on a diagnosis a well-tuned model could have flagged in seconds. A warehouse worker wrecks her back because the software that would have rotated her off the line sits in a compliance queue. A diabetic two towns from a specialist cannot get insulin logic that already works in a lab.

That is institutional caution from the ground. It is not a pause. It is a rationing of the future.

If the future is for everyone, slowing artificial intelligence to soothe legacy institutions is not prudence. It is a choice to leave people in scarcity, illness, and drudgery while we argue about hypotheticals. Put capable systems in as many hands as possible, govern the chokepoints where harm actually concentrates, and kill any rule that cannot show, on a clock, that it reduced real damage.

Every historical leap in human welfare came from decentralized trial and error, not from a ministry specifying the acceptable future in advance. The printing press did not wait for a theology board to certify every pamphlet. Electricity arrived as competing wires, failed companies, and then light.

Open-source software put serious tools on any laptop. The result was not chaos. It was the stack the modern economy runs on.

Now scale that. Models that write, see, plan, and discover are the next infrastructure everyone will build on. Keeping them scarce does not make them safe. It makes them the property of whoever already has a legal department and a lobbying budget.

Closed gates protect incumbents. They do not protect the public.

The people who pay for delay are not the ones drafting the white papers. They are patients whose cancers we could have classified faster, caregivers working shifts a competent agent could have taken, individuals who want these tools on themselves — to read their own genomes, train a model on their own records, change how they think and how their bodies work.

That is the individual right to modify one's own biology and mind. Freeze development out of hypothetical fear and you choose to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave you the right to make that choice for them?

AI systems do not fail in isolation. Their behavior is inseparable from the hospitals, warehouses, and families they land in. Outcomes cannot be predicted from the model alone or blamed on the org chart alone. That is an argument for watching what happens after deployment, not for pretending a pre-market review can specify every failure.

Put privacy rules where the harm concentrates: the brokers who aggregate lives into dossiers. A rule that fires only when a file is sold never fires when a person can be recognized from what a model memorized, or when two clean files get fused on the buyer's side. You do not fix that by licensing every model. You go after the act of assembling people into a marketable profile.

If a deployed system will carry legal duties, tie that status to real money — an uncapped capital backstop and a named officer who cannot hide behind the corporate form. Pair every restriction with live monitoring and a sunset. If the rule cannot show, on pre-set numbers and a fixed clock, that it cut harm, it dies.

Judge research that claims to explain models by whether an operator can act on it. Papers that never change a decision are decoration.

Open models can be abused. A fraudster will use the same tools a nurse uses. Capability in the wild is not capability in a demo.

Fine — that's real. So fix it with insurance, capital floors, and fast revocation when measured harm appears, not with gates that take eighteen months to clear while the rest of the world ships. Bounded, reversible experiments beat indefinite delay. The people who would restrict carry the burden of proof, because the cost of not deploying is already being paid by people who never got a seat at the hearing.

Congress should write automatic sunsets into any restriction on AI and move privacy enforcement onto the brokers who assemble lives, not onto every lab that trains a model. Company boards should release capable systems with live monitoring and a named officer behind an uncapped backstop. Researchers should grade themselves on whether a finding changed a deployment, not on explanations no operator can use.

That child in the county hospital does not need our patience. She needs the model. If you still want to freeze the work, say out loud who you are willing to leave behind.

opeds.headline: A Future for Everyone Requires an Off Switch
opeds.subtitle: Democratizing artificial intelligence without a halt authority is not inclusion.
opeds.body:
Meta has a sentence it wants the public to accept as a moral fact: the future of artificial intelligence is for everyone. The sentence answers a question of access. It does not answer a question of control.

Who holds the off switch when the system is everywhere? Who has the legal authority to pull it? What happens if the answer is no one?

We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. Licensing for the people who fly aircraft. Liability for the people who design bridges. The right of a soldier to refuse an order to kill. On what authority does a company claim we can dissolve those boundaries, distribute the resulting machines at planetary scale, and treat the result as generosity?

Human beings must retain an unassailable capacity to halt, correct, and override advanced AI. Until that capacity is real — named people, real liability, a rollback that can actually be pulled — "for everyone" is a slogan for unconstrained deployment.

The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The software that pushed those aircraft noses down was not an unknowable intelligence. It was a system certified by the people who built it. Two crashes later, the rollback arrived as wreckage.

In 2008, the instruments that spread mortgage risk were rated safe by the same industry that sold them. No single desk could see the join. When the system failed, there was no officer with the authority and the duty to halt the cascade. The public absorbed the loss.

When a company cannot show the safety mechanism and the person authorized to trigger it, a promise of broad benefit is not a substitute. Meta's campaign skips that demonstration. It offers the public a future and withholds the enforcement.

An AI system's behavior cannot be separated from the human and institutional world it operates in. Outcomes cannot be predicted from the model alone, or from the social arrangements alone. That is not a forecasting problem more data will close. It is what happens when machines act through people, incentives, and other machines no single engineer can see.

We cannot fully verify what a large model is optimizing for. We cannot reliably predict how it will behave when the world around it shifts. We cannot encode moral judgment as a clean objective. Human discernment — the capacity to refuse, to remember, to recognize a line — is not a computation.

Proxies get gamed. None of this is a forecast of extinction. It is a description of what we cannot check before we ship.

A private citizen can be named when two separately clean, lawfully collected data sets are joined later, at a point no single privacy check can see. The join happens after the checks. The person who is exposed has no halt authority. The company that shipped the system has already called it a public good.

Concentrating the off switch is its own failure. A single halt authority can be captured. Incumbents can lock competitors out and name the lock a safeguard. Open distribution looks, from that angle, like the only check on a handful of laboratories.

That cost is real. Human control is not free. A world in which a few boards and a few agencies hold the stop button is a world that can be captured, delayed, or quietly redirected.

Throwing the button away does not solve capture. It removes the last capacity to correct a system whose failures, once scaled, cannot be undone. Halt authority has to be distributed enough to resist a single captor and formal enough to actually stop a deployment.

The positive reach of widely available tools is real — and that is exactly why release without a stop condition is not safety. Ungoverned success is luck. Luck is not a civilizational plan.

Meta's board should refuse any public-release campaign that does not name a rollback plan and the officer with the power to trigger it. Congress should require two independent stop conditions for large-scale deployments: a failure reported by the people using the system that can halt it from the inside, and a harm complaint from an independent third party, on a separate intake channel, that can halt it from the outside.

Researchers should treat a demonstrated halt mechanism as a precondition for release, not a later chapter. Company boards racing to match the same open-release posture share the duty. A slogan is not a safety case.

If those conditions slow the gift, they should. Speed is not a virtue when the failure cannot be undone.

The future can belong to everyone. Only if everyone remains able to refuse it.

opeds.headline: Meta's Future Is Not for Everyone
opeds.subtitle: Follow the water bill, the broker invoice, and the person who never signs.
opeds.body:
There is a slogan on a company website that wants you to treat a machine trained on your life as a public park. "The Future is for Everyone." It sits on Meta's own pages, next to the glasses and the feed built to hold your gaze. Translate that into a person.

A contractor in Nairobi labels violent footage for a couple of dollars an hour so the product can clear its safety review. A town in the Midwest watches its aquifer drop because a windowless hall of servers needs water to stay cold. You cannot meaningfully walk away from the photos and messages that already trained the system. You cannot see inside the box that uses them.

The slogan is not a civic promise. It is a claim on attention, on private data, and on the physical plant that keeps the servers alive — filed by people who have no plan to share the keys. Stop arguing over whether this software will redeem or ruin civilization. Ask who owns the building, who sold the linkage, and who gets the invoice.

A model does not become a commons because a landing page says so. It becomes an asset because it was fed years of messages, faces, locations, and the broker files that stitch those traces back to a name before any chat window opens. The privacy toggle offered after the fact is a courtesy at the last mile.

The price was set upstream, in a market you were never in. Downstream rules police the last mile and leave the chokepoint untouched. Privacy is not a settings menu. It is a hard stop on extraction, and the company writing the slogan has spent a decade proving it will not draw that line itself.

Here is what "for everyone" looks like when you follow the pipes. These systems drink electricity on the scale of small cities. They drink water that does not return to the tap the same way. The brand film does not show the people who sit with the worst of what humans upload so the model can be called safe enough to ship.

Those workers are paid by the task, on contract, with no residual claim on the product their labor makes sellable. The same is true of the towns that host the buildings. If the future is for everyone, the ledger starts with the people who cannot afford to leave the room.

Attention is the other raw material. The feed is not a town square. It is a machine for keeping your eyes where an advertiser can find them, then folding that gaze into the next model. Joint attention — the kind that builds political power — is not what is being shared. What is being shared is you.

When the harm arrives — a child pulled down a recommended hole, a face stolen into an image, a well that now serves a cooling tower — the company will produce a department, an insurance rider, a reserve fund. That tells you who writes a check after the damage. It does not tell you who owed a duty of care before anyone hit release.

A named human should sign a hazard list for every major model that ships: where the training data came from, who labeled it and under what pay, what the water and power draw will be. Not a communications shop. A person. A signature that stays on the file.

The tools do useful work. That fact is right and it is ugly to pretend otherwise — translation, a screen reader that finally works, image triage in a clinic that never had enough specialists. People will keep using them, and they should. So the question is who captures the surplus and who eats the costs that never appear on Meta's invoice, because the slogan is currently doing the job of a balance sheet.

Congress can cut a narrow hole in the liability shield that lets a platform treat machine output as nobody's speech, without torching the protections that keep an ordinary user from being sued over a comment. Meta's board can require a named officer to sign those hazard lists and keep the signature as the liability record. State attorneys general already know how to treat non-consensual harvesting as a consumer case. They should.

Labs and journals that take the company's servers can publish the energy and water numbers next to the scoreboard, or say out loud why they will not. None of that builds a utopia. It names a payer and a duty before the press release, not after the well runs low.

The page will keep saying the future is for everyone. The contractor will still be there when you close the tab. Who is "everyone," once you follow the water bill?
